stimulus.text:
Paraphrase of President Lyndon Johnson's commencement address at the University of Michigan, May 22, 1964.

Johnson said, "The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time. But that is just the beginning." He named three places to begin building it: "in our cities, in our countryside, and in our classrooms." He added that the Great Society "is not a safe harbor, a resting place, a final objective, a finished work. It is a challenge constantly renewed."

rationales.A: Johnson names classrooms as one of three national building places, not as a private family matter.
rationales.B: Background: Johnson says in the speech that in the classrooms of America, children's lives will be shaped.
rationales.C: Cities, countryside, and classrooms are all named as building places, so none is ranked below the others.
rationales.D: Johnson treats classrooms as a place to build the Great Society, not as a cost the nation cannot afford.
rationales.general:
1. Johnson names three building places, and classrooms are one of them.
2. A building place is where the Great Society takes shape, so classrooms carry real weight.
3. Background: Johnson says in the speech that in the classrooms, children's lives will be shaped.
4. Education is therefore a foundation of the vision, not a side item.
Remember: What a speaker lists as a building place is a foundation, not a detail.
